game.title: Bake the Fraction Feast
game.request: Create a fractions game based on baking that teaches 4th graders to compare and add simple fractions

spec.title: Bake the Fraction Feast
spec.description: Help a baker compare and add simple fractions to finish tasty recipes. Each stage uses baking steps to practice fraction skills with clear feedback.
spec.subject: Math
spec.learning_objective: Compare and add simple fractions with like denominators in real-world baking situations.
spec.controls: Read the story, choose the best answer, and move through each baking stage.

stages.title: Measuring the Batter
stages.story: You are helping measure ingredients for a cake. The recipe needs careful fraction choices so the batter turns out right.

questions.q: The recipe uses 1/4 cup of sugar and 2/4 cup of flour. Which amount is larger?
questions.explanation: 2/4 is greater than 1/4 because both fractions have the same denominator, and 2 is larger than 1.

questions.q: Which fraction is equal to 3/4 cup?
questions.explanation: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4 because the denominators are the same, so you add the numerators.

stages.title: Fruit for the Pie
stages.story: Next, you are adding fruit to a pie filling. You need to combine fractions to make the correct amount.

questions.q: A pie needs 1/8 cup of strawberries and 3/8 cup of blueberries. How much fruit is that altogether?
questions.explanation: 1/8 + 3/8 = 4/8. When denominators are the same, add the numerators.

questions.q: Which is greater?
questions.explanation: 5/6 is greater than 2/6 because the denominators are the same and 5 is larger than 2.

stages.title: Decorating the Cupcakes
stages.story: The cupcakes need frosting and sprinkles. Compare the fractions to decide which topping amount is bigger.

questions.q: Which amount of frosting is more?
questions.explanation: 3/5 is greater than 2/5 because the denominators are the same and 3 is larger than 2.

questions.q: The baker used 1/3 cup of chocolate chips and then added 1/3 cup more. How much chocolate chips were used in all?
questions.explanation: 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3. Add the numerators and keep the denominator the same.
